chapters.1: Amos, a shepherd from Judah, pronounces God's judgment on surrounding nations—Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, and Edom—for their violence and cruelty, especially toward Israel, promising each will be destroyed by fire.
chapters.2: The judgment oracles continue against Moab, Ammon, and even Judah itself for abandoning God's law, before turning to Amos's main target, Israel, condemned for exploiting the poor and corrupting the Nazirites and prophets despite all God had done for them in the past.
chapters.3: Amos explains that Israel's special relationship with God means greater accountability, not immunity, comparing his prophetic warning to a lion's roar that cannot be ignored. He announces that an enemy will besiege the land and strip its palaces and altars.
chapters.4: God recalls sending droughts, blight, and plagues to try to turn Israel back to him, but the people refused to repent each time. Amos warns them to prepare to meet their God in judgment since lesser warnings have failed.
chapters.5: Amos laments Israel's coming downfall and urges the people to seek the Lord and genuine justice rather than empty religious ritual. He declares that God hates their feasts and sacrifices while they ignore righteousness, famously calling for justice to roll like a river.
chapters.6: Amos pronounces woe on those who live in luxury and ease while ignoring the nation's coming ruin, describing the wealthy elite's lavish feasting and self-satisfaction. He warns that an enemy nation will soon bring affliction on the whole country.
chapters.7: Amos recounts three visions—locusts, fire, and a plumb line—showing God's patience giving way to a decision to judge Israel decisively. When he confronts the corrupt priest Amaziah at Bethel, Amos insists he is no professional prophet but a herdsman whom God called, and predicts personal disaster for Amaziah's family.
chapters.8: A vision of a basket of ripe summer fruit signals that Israel's time is up. Amos condemns merchants who cheat the poor and manipulate scales, and warns of a coming "famine" not of food but of hearing God's word, when people will search for it and not find it.
chapters.9: Amos describes a vision of God destroying the corrupt sanctuary and declares that none of the sinful nation can escape his judgment, wherever they hide. The book ends with a surprising turn to hope, promising that God will eventually restore the fallen "tent of David," rebuild the ruined cities, and replant his people securely in their land.
